title: Coming Home Present
tagline: Twelve short sessions on presence after time in a program: reconnect with children and a significant other.
course_purpose: Twelve short film sessions for fathers in rehab or treatment preparing to reconnect with their children and/or a significant other: the body you bring home, the wave, few promises kept, the child who grew, small deposits, repair, reunion day, and the season after. Built so a man can complete the practices inside the rules that govern him now.
audience: Lead audience: fathers in rehab or treatment preparing to reconnect with children and/or a significant other. Practices stay inside the rules that govern him now; where contact is limited, every drill has a before-return option. Completion never requires child contact.
facilitator_note: Self-paced film. About twelve minutes each. Watch when you can. A Certified Facilitator is available for questions and accountability when your seat is claimed. Optional live cohorts may be offered by some programs. Lead scenes are the treatment house, program rules, early leave passes, first calls home, first visit, and first night back. The reunion session is a climax: you leave with a first-hour plan for kids and/or a significant other, rehearsed and in hand. Logged sessions and a checkable practice. Completion never requires contact with your child, and no practice ever asks you to go beyond the rules that govern you now or any court order. Where contact is limited, every drill has a before-return option.

sessions.title: The Body You Bring Home
sessions.keyline: Your body did its job there. Now teach it that home is not there.
sessions.one_scene: Quiet hours in the treatment house. A door slams down the hall. Before a thought arrives, his shoulders are up and his eyes are on the doorway. Same body that will walk into a loud kitchen on his first night home.
sessions.in_the_room: The body's alarm in plain language: how a long stretch in a controlled environment (program or facility) retunes it, and how that collides with a loud home and a waiting significant other. You plot your baseline and pick your tells.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can name what your body is doing when it revs, and call it a physical response, not a character flaw.
sessions.practice: Keep a short body-state log and name two likely home triggers.
sessions.science_or_note: Fight or flight can outlast the threat; naming the response is the first retraining step.

choices: Forgetting that time completely

checkpoint_questions.prompt: A loud noise at home spikes you to full alert. What does this session call that?
choices: A character flaw

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What is the daily practice this session gives you?
choices: Avoiding stressful rooms
A slow exhale practice that tells your body the threat level here
Pushing through and ignoring the surge

sessions.after_return: Keep the log at home, agree one signal with a family member if contact allows, and report what happened.

sessions.title: Home Is Not There
sessions.keyline: Same noise, new meaning. Train the difference.
sessions.one_scene: On the house phone he hears a shout in the background. His body tags it as danger. On the next early leave pass he labels the same sound: kid looking for a shoe. Same noise. New meaning. Shoulders stay down.
sessions.in_the_room: You train the difference between there (program rules, high alert) and home with concrete sounds and scenes. Rehearsal gives the body a new meaning before the live test.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can catch a home sound and label it as home on purpose.
sessions.practice: Name two home sounds that used to mean threat and rehearse a calm home label for each.
sessions.science_or_note: Retraining meaning reduces false alarms when old cues meet a safe setting.

sessions.after_return: When one of those sounds hits, say the home label once under your breath and log whether your body stood down.

sessions.title: Plan Around the Wave
sessions.keyline: Plan around the wave. Do not grade yourself by it.
sessions.one_scene: Day nine after his first overnight pass. He slept badly, snapped over spilled cereal, and by noon he is quietly deciding he is failing his kids and his partner. He is not failing. He is in a wave, and the plan says what to do on wave days.
sessions.in_the_room: Energy, mood, and sleep run in waves in the early weeks of any return from a program. That is expected. You plan around it instead of reading it as a verdict on the reconnect.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can expect the low weeks, plan around them, and stop grading yourself by them.
sessions.practice: Write a wave-day rule: sleep anchor, fewer commitments, and one recovery move.
sessions.science_or_note: Early-return waves in sleep and mood are common while a body leaves an imposed routine.

sessions.after_return: Hold the same sleep anchor at home and use the wave-day rule on the next hard day.

sessions.title: Few Promises, Kept
sessions.one_scene: He wants to promise everything on the first call home. He picks two standing call times the program phone will allow, and keeps both. By week three his child and his significant other stop asking if he means it.
sessions.in_the_room: Distance and early return punish over-promising. You choose a short list you can keep from where you actually are (program rules, court orders), then keep it without fail.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can make fewer promises and keep every one you make.
sessions.practice: Choose at most three commitments you can keep this week and keep a written record.
sessions.science_or_note: Reliability beats volume; each kept promise is evidence.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Which plan fits the first weeks, per this session?
choices: Pack the calendar to make up for lost time

choices: Children prefer silence

script_aids.purpose: Install reliability as the trust currency: few promises, kept without fail.
script_aids.emotional_beat: Discipline over guilt: pride in two kept times instead of shame about not doing everything.

sessions.title: The Child Who Grew
sessions.keyline: Meet the child in front of you, not the one you left.
sessions.one_scene: On a permitted call from the house, the child talks about a teacher he has never heard of and a best friend whose name is new. He left a child who held his hand crossing the street. He meets the one on the line now.
sessions.in_the_room: You map where your child actually is now against the child you left, then build questions that rebuild a current picture: friends, fears, interests. You also note what your significant other has been carrying.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can recalibrate to the child who exists today.
sessions.practice: Build a one-page current picture and draft questions that are only questions.
sessions.science_or_note: Children hit growth milestones on a clock; knowing the present child is the base of attunement.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Who does this session tell you to get to know?
choices: The child you remember

sessions.title: Ask Before You Assume
sessions.keyline: Ask once. Listen longer than you talk.
sessions.one_scene: On the first visit, he almost fills the silence with advice for his partner and his child. He asks one real question instead, then shuts up long enough to hear the answer. They talk more in two minutes than in the last month of lectures.
sessions.in_the_room: Assumptions belong to the people you left. You practice one clean ask and a longer listen with your child and/or significant other, then reflect one thing you heard.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can ask once and listen longer than you talk.
sessions.practice: Ask one real question and reflect one thing you heard without fixing.
sessions.science_or_note: Listening longer than you talk rebuilds a current map of the child and the home.

sessions.title: Small Deposits
sessions.keyline: Small and often beats big and rare.
sessions.one_scene: Mid-conversation with his significant other on an early leave pass, the child appears holding a drawing. He stops, looks at it, and says show me the best part. Twenty seconds. That is a deposit.
sessions.in_the_room: Trust rebuilds through many small responsive interactions with kids and partner, not one big make-up moment. You practice catching and returning bids for attention.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can make daily small deposits and explain why they beat grand gestures.
sessions.practice: Catch and return three bids, or role-play five exchanges if contact is limited.
sessions.science_or_note: Serve and return: a child's bid met by a steady adult builds trust and brains.

sessions.title: Frequency Beats Intensity
sessions.one_scene: He used to wait for a perfect long visit after discharge. He switches to short, on-time calls the program schedule allows. The child starts setting a place for the call without being asked. His partner stops bracing for a miss.
sessions.in_the_room: Predictable short contact beats rare dramatic presence. You design a frequency you can keep from where you stand: program phone rules, court orders.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can show up short and steady on a schedule the child and partner can trust.
sessions.practice: Set one repeatable short contact ritual inside the rules that govern you now.
sessions.science_or_note: Predictability lowers a child's background stress more than occasional intensity.

script_aids.emotional_beat: Relief for men who cannot deliver epic time yet: steadiness is enough to start.

sessions.title: When It Breaks
sessions.keyline: Rupture is normal. Repair is the skill.
sessions.one_scene: He promised a call at seven. The house phone line ran long and the call went out at nine. The next call opens with the repair to his child and his partner, said plainly, no excuses attached.
sessions.in_the_room: Every close relationship ruptures. Repair, not perfection, builds security with kids and a significant other. You practice a plain repair script until it comes out steady.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can come back after a bad moment and repair it out loud.
sessions.practice: Write a repair for one past rupture and rehearse it aloud.
sessions.science_or_note: Reliable repair, not perfection, is what builds security.

sessions.title: Repair Without Pride
sessions.one_scene: Pride wants him to wait for his significant other to cool off after a hard call. He goes first instead: I was wrong to raise my voice. You did not deserve that. Short. No defense. The air changes.
sessions.in_the_room: You practice going first with a short repair toward your child and/or partner. Pride delays the skill; going first protects the bond.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can go first with a short repair when pride wants to wait.
sessions.practice: Write a go-first repair in under twenty words and deliver or rehearse it.
sessions.science_or_note: Going first models responsibility; delay teaches the other person to carry the silence.

sessions.title: Reunion Day
sessions.keyline: If the child pulls away, that is the start, not the answer.
sessions.one_scene: First hour home after the program. The younger one hides behind a leg. The older one shrugs off the hug. His significant other is careful, not cold. He keeps his voice low and offers the small plan he rehearsed: a walk to the corner and back, nothing more.
sessions.in_the_room: You prepare for the first hours back with kids and/or a significant other, including early pull-away. You write and rehearse a low-pressure first-hour plan.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You leave with a realistic, rehearsed first-hour plan and the patience to let it be imperfect.
sessions.practice: Write and rehearse a low-pressure first-hour plan.
sessions.science_or_note: Early pull-away at reunions is common and often temporary; patience is a skill.

sessions.title: The Season of Return
sessions.keyline: The return is a season, not a day.
sessions.one_scene: Week six after discharge, an ordinary Tuesday. Nothing dramatic happened. He did the ritual with the kids, checked in with his partner, logged the wave, made the small deposit. That is the plan working.
sessions.in_the_room: You fold the course into a personal return plan for fathering and partner reconnect, frame the work as a long season, and name an accountability partner.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You leave with a written season plan, a first checkpoint, and a named accountability partner.
sessions.practice: Complete a one-page return plan with a checkpoint date and named accountability partner.
sessions.science_or_note: Routines hold gains; steady spaced practice beats bursts.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What is the return, in this course's final frame?
choices: A day you get right or wrong
A season you work, deposit by deposit
A test the child administers

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What carries the return through month three and beyond?
choices: The emotion of the reunion
The routines: standing times, kept promises, fast repairs
The child's forgiveness

checkpoint_questions.prompt: When the old pattern gets tested and you hold, what does the session call that?
choices: Luck
The line holding, which is what change looks like from inside
A sign the work is finished

script_aids.purpose: Close by converting skills into a written season plan for fathering and partner reconnect, with accountability.
script_aids.practical_insight: The return is a season, not a day.
script_aids.emotional_beat: Quiet confidence: ordinary Tuesday faithfulness is the win.
shape_motifs: calendar season band, not a single starred day
ritual ticks continuing past week six
one-page plan card with checkpoint mark
two linked dots for accountability
do_not: Do not lead with deployment, combat, or barracks as the default scene
Prefer treatment house, program rules, early leave passes, first calls, first visit, first night back
No faces, bodies, photographic people, or culture-specific dress
Do not invent doctrine that conflicts with keyline, practice, or checkpoints
Keep practices inside the rules that govern the man now
Do not require child contact for completion drills
Do not treat reunion pull-away as final rejection
script_aids.bridge_from_prev: First-hour plan is ready; widen it into the months that carry the return.
script_aids.bridge_to_next: Course close: keep the written plan and facilitator or partner check-ins.

sessions.before_return: Complete the one-page return plan, name the accountability partner, and set the first after-return checkpoint date.
sessions.after_return: Work the plan and report at the checkpoint.

final_qa.prompt: Describe your body's alarm firing at home or in rehearsal since you started this course: the trigger, what the old response would have been, and what you did instead.
List the small deposits you have running right now: what you promised, to which child and/or significant other, and your record of keeping each one. What is the next deposit you will add?
Write your first-hour plan for the reunion, or describe how the first hour actually went: the setting, your opening move with kids and/or your significant other, and your plan if a child pulls away.
Name the few promises you are keeping this season, and the accountability partner or facilitator check-in that holds you to them.
